newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Arafat urges Europe, United States to guard peace.
newsitem.headline: Arafat urges Europe, United States to guard peace.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat called on Europe and the United States on Tuesday to save the Middle East peace process from what he termed continual breaches of agreements by Israel.

Speaking after talks with Morocco's King Hassan, at which he said the two leaders agreed on the need for an urgent meeting of the Jerusalem Committee, Arafat said expanded Israel's plans for more settlements would have a "very negative reaction" on the whole peace process.
He added: "This is a big challenge for the peace process and will harm the whole peace process.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said earlier in the day he would convene a ministerial committee on Jerusalem on Wednesday to approve a plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews in Har Homa, known as Jabal Abu Ghneim by Arabs, a hill taken over by Israel in the 1967 Middle East War.
"I want to clarify unequivocally; we will build in all Jerusalem," the Israeli leader said.
Arafat, reacting to Netayahu, told reporters at Rabat airport: "First of all what is going on is a clear breaching of what has been agreed.
"Not only that, it is illegal and against the United Nations and the letter of guarantee signed... in Madrid (peace conference) and against all that was agreed in Oslo."

He added: "He (Netanyahu) has to understand, and all the Israeli leadership must understand, that (for) settlements in Hebron or Jerusalem or outside Jerusalem, its target is against the peace process..."
Their aim, said Arafat, was to make "geopolitical and demographic change in the city which is completely against the peace process."
The Palestinian leader arrived earlier in the day from Brussels where he had called on European Union countries for more political backing. He is due to visit the United States early next month.
Asked what he expected from the EU and Washington for the Middle East, he said: "Protect the peace process from this continual challenge."

The Palestinians were not asking "for the moon" but wanted Israel to stick to earlier agreements. "Otherwise there will be a very negative reaction not only in the peace process on our (Palestinian-Israeli) track, but on the whole process in our area," he said.

Commenting on his talks with King Hassan, Arafat said these were "very positive" and went into "details of the breachings from the Israeli side in Jerusalem and around Jerusalem against the Palestinians, Christians and Moslems in the holy city, and the necessity for an urgent meeting of the Jerusalem Committee to discuss these very dangerous and serious events."
The Palestinian leader, after being held up briefly by fog, later left for Ghaza. REUTER
